content: Small and medium businesses need Mashbot to manage their presence across multiple social networks through a consistent service. Staff should be able to connect external accounts, prepare campaigns, schedule content for simultaneous publication, manage contributor, approver, and publisher roles, respond to audience activity, and monitor keywords and campaign history. The service should reduce the effort required to coordinate marketing and customer engagement across changing platforms.

The main goal is to keep our messaging consistent across all the channels while saving time for the team. We want to publish campaigns in one place, reach customers where they actually are, and respond quickly when they comment, ask questions, or mention us. It also helps us coordinate marketing work and customer engagement without having to jump between different platforms all day.

Right now we definitely need the major ones like Facebook, Instagram, X, and LinkedIn, since those are the ones we use most for campaigns and customer interaction. Depending on the client, we may also want to support TikTok and maybe YouTube later, but that’s more of a future need than an immediate one. We’d also want to handle both business pages and any account types that let us publish or reply on behalf of the brand.

Usually one person drafts the content or response, then another person reviews it, and someone with publishing rights sends it out. For campaigns, it’s a similar flow: a contributor prepares the materials, an approver checks brand and compliance, and then a publisher schedules or posts it. For customer responses, we’d want the same kind of handoff, so a message can be assigned, reviewed if needed, and then answered without losing track of who did what.

Yes, we’d want fairly clear role separation. Marketing staff should be able to draft and prepare campaigns, support staff should mainly handle monitoring and replying to audience activity, and managers should be able to review, approve, and oversee everything, including seeing the full history. Publishing should stay limited to specific authorized users, because we need control over what goes live and when.

We’d want it to surface the problem clearly right away, with enough detail for the team to understand whether it was a scheduling issue, a network error, or something like a permissions problem. For publishing, if something fails, it should be easy to retry or reschedule without losing the content or the audit trail. For audience engagement, if a reply can’t be sent, we’d want the item left in a queue or flagged so someone can pick it up quickly instead of it disappearing.

If something is rejected or flagged for a policy issue, it should not go out as-is, and the team should be able to see exactly why it was blocked. The contributor and approver need to be notified, and a manager should be able to review it if there’s any question or if an exception is possible. Ideally the item stays in draft or needs revision status until someone fixes it and sends it back through approval.

We’d want it to be very reliable, because scheduled posts and monitoring are core day-to-day work. Short interruptions could be acceptable as long as they’re rare and we’re alerted quickly, but we can’t really tolerate missed publish windows or long gaps in monitoring without some kind of retry or catch-up. If there’s a brief outage, the system should recover cleanly and show us what was delayed or missed.

For critical campaigns, we’d prefer to hold the campaign rather than automatically reroute it somewhere unexpected. If the primary publishing path fails, the system should retry first and then keep it queued with an alert so a person can decide whether to wait, reschedule, or use another approved account. Automatic failover would only be acceptable if it’s fully controlled and pre-approved, because we don’t want anything to publish on the wrong brand account by accident.

Yes, that’s the behavior we’d want. It should retry automatically for a short period, then catch up on anything still pending once the service is back, and clearly mark what went through, what was delayed, and what still needs a person to review. We’d also want a visible log or status view so the team can see the impact without having to piece it together manually.

We’d probably need some basic organization and user records as well, like company profile details, team members, and which social accounts belong to which business unit or brand. It would also help to keep approval settings, notification preferences, and maybe a simple activity or audit log for who changed what and when. I’m not sure we need anything much beyond that unless you’re counting billing or subscription information, which would be handled separately if included.

Yes, one person should be able to belong to multiple groups, because in a small business people often wear more than one hat. Access to social accounts and campaign work should follow the group or brand they’re assigned to, so someone in one unit doesn’t automatically see or manage everything in the organization. If a person has roles in more than one group, the system should combine those permissions in a controlled way, but I’d want the access boundaries to stay clear.

We’d want the basics like company name, primary contact details, timezone, and maybe the main industry or business type, since those affect scheduling and reporting. Things like billing information, legal entity details, or multiple office locations would be optional, and only shown if the business actually needs them. I’d also keep internal notes or admin-only fields hidden from regular users.

Each external social account should be tied to its specific network, and the system should only offer actions that network actually supports. So if one platform doesn’t allow a certain kind of post, reply, or reporting metric, Mashbot should hide or disable that option rather than letting users try it and fail later. We’d also want the system to make the differences obvious up front when a campaign is being prepared, so staff can adjust content before scheduling it.

If the action is supported only in some cases, I’d expect Mashbot to show it when it’s available for that account and content type, but disable it with a clear reason when the setup doesn’t meet the requirements. If it’s never available for that network or role, then hiding it is probably better so the interface stays clean. For reporting, I’d still want the view to exist, but with missing metrics called out clearly instead of pretending the data is complete.

It should be available only when the account is connected, the user has the right role, and the content type matches what that network allows. If one of those pieces is missing but the action could work in another setup, then disable it and say what’s missing, like “publisher role required” or “this network doesn’t support video posts.” If it can never apply to that network or that user category, then hide it so people aren’t distracted by options they can’t use.

Approvals should be configurable by organization, brand, or campaign, because some teams will want stricter control than others. Usually a contributor creates the content, an approver reviews it, and only publishers can actually send it out, but we’d want the rule to require approval only when that team chooses it or when a sensitive network or campaign is involved. Exceptions should be limited and visible in the audit log, and if someone overrides an approval step, the system should record who did it and why.

Yes, billing and subscription details should be tightly restricted, probably only to organization admins or a designated finance role. I’d keep those settings separate from brand and campaign work so regular marketing users don’t see them unless they need to. Any changes there should be audited, and for important changes like plan upgrades or payment method updates, an approval or confirmation step would be a good idea.

I’d allow maybe a senior operations manager or system admin to view billing details if they need to help with account setup or troubleshooting, but not necessarily edit payment methods. They should probably be able to see the current plan and renewal status, but sensitive things like card numbers, invoices with tax details, or cancellation controls should stay restricted. If a team is acting in a support role, I’d want read-only access with strong auditing rather than full management rights.

For those roles, I’d treat access as read-only by default and require a separate approval step before any sensitive change is made. Plan upgrades, payment method updates, and cancellations should all be logged with who requested it, who approved it, and when it happened, and I’d want a confirmation from an organization admin or finance owner before anything goes through. If it’s an urgent support case, we could allow a temporary override, but only with a reason recorded and a clear audit trail.

That should stay limited to finance or organization admins. Contributors, approvers, and publishers shouldn’t normally see invoice or payment history, since it’s not part of their campaign work, and I’d avoid letting them request copies directly from the system unless there’s a very specific business need. If they do need something for a reimbursement or procurement process, it should go through an admin or finance contact instead.

Those credentials should always be protected, and in practice only a very small admin or security role should ever be able to see or reset them. Most users should only be able to reconnect the account through an approved reauthorization flow, not view the actual password or token. If troubleshooting or recovery is needed, I’d want a time-limited exception with explicit approval, full logging, and ideally the secret never shown in plain text unless there’s no other option.

Yes, there can be, especially for customer messages and keyword monitoring where privacy rules vary by region. We’d need the system to respect country or region-based restrictions if a client operates in multiple jurisdictions, and in some cases limit who can view message content based on consent or internal policy. I don’t know the exact legal thresholds yet, so that would need to be confirmed with the compliance team.

The main reason is to spot brand mentions, campaign performance, and customer issues early so the team can respond quickly and adjust content. Day to day, most people should only see the keywords and history for the brands or campaigns they’re assigned to, and they should be able to review trends or comments but not change historical records. Only managers or approvers should be able to adjust monitoring rules or mark items as resolved when there’s a customer or reputation issue.

I’d want the interaction history to stay tied to the original campaign record even if the campaign gets renamed or reassigned, because we need an accurate audit trail. The visible name can change, but the underlying campaign ID and history should not, so reporting still reflects what happened at the time. If a campaign is split or materially restructured, then we’d probably need a new campaign record rather than rewriting the old history.

They should see the key capability differences up front while they’re drafting the campaign, so they can avoid surprises at publish time. For example, if one network doesn’t support a certain media type, threaded replies, or a specific call-to-action, that should be flagged before scheduling, along with any metric differences in reporting. I’d keep it practical and content-focused rather than exposing every technical detail.

By default, they should only see the brands and campaigns assigned to them, because that matches the way the work is organized and keeps things properly scoped. Broader monitoring across other accounts should be limited to supervisors, managers, or admins who need a cross-account view for oversight. Editing rules, resolving items, or exporting the history should be separate permissions, and I’d only grant those to people who are responsible for managing the monitoring process or reporting to clients.

Yes, there should be filters so we only ingest items that are relevant to accounts and campaigns we actually manage. Private content that we’re not authorized to access, duplicates, and anything tied to an unmanaged account should be ignored, and very late-arriving events might be excluded from alerting if they’re no longer actionable. For reporting, though, I’d still want the system to keep a record of what was received and why it was skipped.

Operationally, I’d expect different handling depending on the reason. If something is unauthorized or unmanaged, it should be skipped entirely and not notify anyone beyond maybe an internal error log; if it’s a duplicate or too late to act on, it can still be ingested for history but should skip alerting. A late or duplicate item might still be kept if it helps with audit trail or if a manager wants to review patterns later, but it shouldn’t reopen the normal response workflow unless someone manually flags it.

Retention should mostly follow the client’s contract and any legal or compliance rules we need to respect, because some customers will want a longer history for reporting and others won’t. Access to those audit records should be restricted to the same roles that can see the related brand or campaign, with admins or compliance users only if we explicitly need that oversight. If the content is private, unauthorized, or otherwise sensitive, I’d want it masked or limited as much as possible while still keeping enough detail for the audit trail.

I’d say redact or mask as soon as the content is private, clearly sensitive, or we’re not fully authorized to store the full text, but still keep the event metadata and a reference to what happened. The unmasked version should be limited to a very small group, like admins or compliance reviewers, and only if they have a business reason to investigate. Regular campaign staff should see enough to understand the event without exposing the full content.

If there’s a legal hold or an active compliance investigation, the record should be kept longer than the normal contract period, even if the client would otherwise be offboarded. On the other hand, if the client asks for deletion and there’s no legal or operational reason to retain it, we should shorten the retention to match the agreed disposal timeline. For offboarding, I’d expect the system to preserve only what’s required for transition, billing, or legal obligations, and then purge the rest.

Anything that breaks publishing, account connection, or incoming engagement handling should be treated as urgent and handled immediately, because it affects day-to-day operations. Changes that only impact reporting details, optional metadata, or noncritical convenience features can usually wait for a later update. If the platform changes access rules or deprecates an API in a way that could stop us from ingesting data or posting on behalf of clients, that would force an immediate operational response.

If publishing succeeds but a related piece like replies or ingestion fails, I’d still keep the core campaign running and mark the affected part as degraded rather than stopping everything. We should retry automatically for transient issues, but escalate immediately if the failure persists, affects multiple accounts, or blocks a role that’s needed for approval or publishing. The key is to separate a full outage from a partial one so staff can keep working with a clear warning that something needs attention.

The audit log should record who bypassed or overrode the approval, when it happened, which campaign or item it affected, and the reason they gave. It should also capture what approval rule was in force at the time and whether the action was within their role’s authority or required an exception. If there was a system suggestion or warning that they ignored, I’d want that saved too so we can reconstruct why the decision was made.

An override should be allowed without escalation only when the person has explicit authority for that account or campaign type, like a designated publisher or manager acting within their assigned limits. If the override goes beyond their authority, it should require a second approval from someone higher up or a documented exception process with a clear reason and timestamp. I’d also expect the system to block the action until that extra approval is recorded, unless there’s an emergency setting we’ve already agreed is available.

Users should be able to save it as pending and notify the approver right away, so the request doesn’t get lost. After approval comes through, they should be able to retry without re-entering everything, as long as nothing about the content or target account has changed. I’d expect some blocks to be immediate and non-bypassable, like when the account is disconnected, the platform has hard policy restrictions, or the content is clearly illegal or unauthorized, even if someone claims it’s an emergency.

If the content or target account changes, I’d expect the pending request to be invalidated rather than silently updated, because the approval was based on a specific version. The user should then resubmit it so the approver is reviewing the current state, and the system should show what changed and why the old request no longer applies. If the change is only something minor and non-material, like a typo fix, maybe that could be handled as a fresh review rule, but I’d rather be conservative.

It should capture the exact warning text or code the system showed, the approval rule or exception that was active at that moment, and the user’s role or authority level compared with what the rule allowed. I’d also want the record to show whether the action was permitted normally, allowed only by exception, or technically outside policy but forced through, because those are very different for later review. If possible, store the item version and the timestamp too so we can reconstruct the full decision context.

A request should be invalidated if the change affects what was approved in a meaningful way, like the text, media, destination account, audience targeting, schedule, or any compliance-sensitive setting. If it’s just a minor, non-substantive edit that doesn’t change the message or where it goes, then I’d expect it to continue without a fresh review. In practice, I’d rather err on the side of requiring a new review whenever there’s any doubt, especially for regulated or high-risk accounts.

The change summary should show what was edited, what the previous version was, and what the current version is, in plain language. It should also highlight anything that affects approval, like the target account, scheduled time, media attachments, campaign tags, or audience settings, and clearly flag if the change is only cosmetic versus something material. If possible, it should note who made the last change and when, so the approver can see how fresh the request is.

Material fields should be the ones that can change the meaning, reach, timing, or compliance risk of the post, so things like text content, images or video, target account, audience, schedule, and campaign assignment. Cosmetic fields would be things like spelling fixes, formatting, or other edits that don’t alter the message or destination. For sensitive requests, yes, the summary should be able to redact certain details for users who don’t have clearance, but approvers still need enough information to make a real decision, so I’d only suppress what they’re not authorized to see.

For non-cleared users, I’d hide the actual account identifiers, the full media contents, private campaign names, and any customer or audience data that could identify people. They could still see that something changed, the type of change, who changed it, when it changed, and whether the change is material or cosmetic. Approvers with clearance should see the full before-and-after details they need to judge the request, but if even they lack clearance for some source data, then the system should show a controlled placeholder and require a separate privileged review path.

We still need agreement on who counts as cleared for each kind of content, because marketing, legal, support, and managers may not all need the same visibility. We also need to decide where the line is between acceptable redaction and too little information for approval, since that balance may differ by account or campaign type. And I think we’d need a policy decision on whether exceptions are handled centrally or by each business unit, because that affects how consistent the system will be.

I’d base clearance on both role and assignment, so someone can only see sensitive content if their job needs it and they’re tied to that account or campaign. Marketing would usually see the full draft and performance context, legal would see anything compliance-related and maybe restricted customer-facing language, support would mostly need visibility into replies and cases rather than full campaign assets, and managers would see status and exceptions but not necessarily every sensitive detail. For account-specific content, I’d keep it limited to the people assigned to that account unless there’s a formal override, because that’s the cleanest way to avoid unnecessary exposure.

In practice, I’d say role alone shouldn’t be enough for sensitive work; the person should also be assigned to that account or campaign, or explicitly granted temporary access. A contributor might be able to draft more broadly, but approval and publishing should be much tighter and usually require both the right role and direct assignment. If someone isn’t assigned, they could perhaps view a limited version or make a request for access, but they shouldn’t be able to push something live just because their title fits.

The practical rule should be that the reviewer must still be able to understand the purpose, destination, timing, and risk of the request without guessing. If redaction removes any detail that changes the meaning, compliance impact, or audience reach, then it isn’t sufficient and the request should go to a fuller review path. Since the needed detail can vary by account or campaign type, I’d make the sufficiency threshold configurable by account or campaign policy rather than one fixed rule for everything.

The reviewer should still see the campaign name or a safe label, the channel it will publish to, the scheduled time, the type of content change, the affected account in a non-sensitive form if needed, and enough of the message context to know what the post is trying to say. They should also be able to see who requested it and whether anything material changed since the last version, even if the full media or exact copy is hidden. I’d still escalate if the post involves regulated products, legal holds, public complaints, high-profile accounts, or anything where a redacted detail could materially change the decision.

If a redaction hides anything that affects audience, timing, claim wording, pricing, legal risk, or brand reputation, I’d treat that as escalation-worthy because it could change the approval decision. Redactions that only cover internal notes, non-essential metadata, or unrelated personal identifiers could stay in the normal path if the reviewer still has enough context to judge the post safely. In other words, if the missing detail could reasonably make someone approve or reject it differently, it should be escalated.

If the exception changes access across multiple accounts, affects a sensitive content class, or creates a new approval authority, I’d handle it centrally so there’s one consistent decision and audit trail. If it’s just a one-off within a single business unit and doesn’t expand visibility beyond that unit’s normal scope, then the business unit could handle it locally. Anything that lets someone see or approve more than their standard role should probably be centralized, because those cases carry the highest risk.

In that middle case, I’d still route it to central review if it touches a sensitive content class or increases approval rights, even if it only applies to one business unit. Local teams can make the business case and recommend it, but central should make the final call because the risk is tied to the content sensitivity and permission change, not just the scope. If needed, central could approve it as a temporary exception with an expiration and audit record.

A temporary exception should only be allowed when there’s a real business need, like a launch deadline, staff absence, or an urgent response situation, and when waiting for the normal process would clearly block something important. It should be tightly scoped to one account or campaign, expire automatically after a short period, and be limited to the minimum additional permission needed rather than a blanket role change. I’d also expect a logged reason, who approved it, and a review after the fact so we can confirm it was used appropriately and didn’t become a workaround.

It should end immediately as soon as the original reason no longer exists, and the extra access or approval right should be removed without waiting for the expiry date. If the approved person leaves or the campaign changes in a way that affects the basis for the exception, I’d treat it the same way and require a fresh request rather than a renewal by default. That change should also be logged, and if anything unusual happened while the exception was active, it should trigger a short review to make sure nothing was published outside the intended scope.

Central should revoke it early if the person misuses the access, if there’s any sign of unauthorized publishing or approval activity, or if the scope starts drifting beyond the original account or campaign. I’d also want a review if the campaign changes materially, the business reason disappears, or the exception is repeatedly renewed instead of being resolved through the normal role process. If the exception creates a pattern of risk or confusion, that’s when central should step in rather than just relying on the audit trail.

It should stop immediately if the change alters who is allowed to publish, what content can go out, or which audience or account is covered. A fresh request should be required if the campaign purpose changes, the approved person changes, or the exception would need broader rights than were originally approved. If it’s just a minor scheduling shift with the same people and the same content scope, that could stay within the existing exception.

We’d want an authorization screen rather than collecting the user’s direct login in Mashbot. In practice, the user should be sent through the network’s own consent flow so they can approve what Mashbot can do, and we store the resulting token or connection details. That feels safer and is easier to manage when platforms change their authentication rules.

Yes, a brand may need multiple accounts on the same network, usually when they have separate regional, product, or business unit presences. But we would likely exclude some account types from publishing or replying if the network doesn’t allow it, or if the account is read-only, like certain analytics or advertising-linked accounts. The exact limits would depend on the platform’s API and what permissions we can safely support.

Mashbot should stop all publishing and replying actions on that account immediately if the connection is lost or the token is invalidated. We should keep the saved campaign history, scheduled content, and audit records, but mark the account as disconnected so staff know it needs attention. Yes, the relevant users or administrators should be notified right away, and any queued posts for that account should be held until the connection is restored or the content is reassigned.

A successful migration needs to preserve the business history and make the team able to pick up work without losing context. We’d want past campaigns, published posts, comments or replies if they matter for reference, and the link between content, the account it belonged to, and who approved or published it. Anything sensitive like tokens or passwords should not be migrated as plain data, and if some platforms won’t let us import older records cleanly, that should be called out so we can verify the gaps.

I’d prefer Mashbot allow the team to proceed, but with the gaps clearly flagged. Blocking the migration entirely would be too disruptive if the missing pieces are only historical, as long as the team knows what didn’t come over and can verify it separately. If something essential to current operations is missing, then that should trigger a stronger warning and maybe a manual review before go-live.

It should exclude passwords entirely, and treat any tokens as a special-case manual step rather than migrating them automatically. If a platform gives us a usable authorization token, I’d want Mashbot to vault it securely and never show it in plain text, with the team clearly warned that credentials were handled separately. That keeps us from accidentally importing something unsafe while still allowing a controlled handoff where possible.

The people responsible for that brand’s social operations should be notified, and probably an administrator as well if the account is tied to active campaigns. The notification should say which account was affected, what happened, whether any scheduled posts are on hold, and what action is needed to reconnect it. It should be clear and practical so the team can react quickly without having to dig through logs.

I’d say immediate notification for every disconnect is fine if the account is actually used for publishing or replying. If it’s just an inactive or noncritical connected account, then we could group or delay the alert a bit so people aren’t flooded. The key exception is anything with scheduled posts or active engagement work, because that needs to be surfaced right away.

Yes, Mashbot should respect whatever consent and permission flow each platform requires, even if that means the onboarding steps differ a bit by network. If a platform only grants limited scopes, then Mashbot should only enable the features those permissions allow, and if reauthorization has to be done manually later, that’s acceptable as long as the user is clearly guided through it. I’d also want the system to make it obvious when an account is partially connected versus fully ready.

Users should be able to see the account status, what permissions are missing, and any campaigns or features that will be affected. They should probably still be able to view history and existing linked data, but Mashbot should hold back publishing, replying, or scheduling anything that depends on the missing permission. That way the team understands the limitation without accidentally using an incomplete connection.

In a limited case, yes, if the missing permission doesn’t affect the specific action being taken. For example, if the account can still publish but can’t read analytics, then Mashbot should let publishing continue and just keep the unavailable parts disabled. But if the missing scope touches the exact channel or action, then it should be blocked rather than trying to work around it.

Yes, it should avoid touching anything during scheduled publishing windows, and we’d want a clear blackout period around major campaign launches if possible. Routine updates should be coordinated with whoever manages the campaigns so they can confirm it won’t interfere with posts, approvals, or monitoring. If a change could interrupt service, Mashbot should prefer delaying it rather than risking missed publishes or lost audience responses.

For a major launch, I’d want updates paused long enough beforehand that we’re not making risky changes right before content starts going out, but I don’t have a fixed number of hours or days in mind yet. During that period, anything that could affect publishing, approvals, account connections, or monitoring should be blocked unless it’s a real emergency. An override should be limited to a senior admin or someone specifically designated by the campaign owner, so it doesn’t get bypassed casually.

A valid override would usually be something urgent that protects an active campaign or prevents a missed post, broken connection, or customer-facing issue. If it’s just a convenience change or a noncritical update, I’d expect it to wait until the blackout ends. Even with authorization, I’d still deny anything that would create a real risk of corrupting scheduled content, breaking an in-progress approval chain, or causing duplicated or unintended publishes.

Mashbot should surface those as related items so the team can see they’re connected, rather than treating each one as totally separate. If one response is going out on a network, it should help avoid duplicate replies and show the team where a coordinated answer is needed on the other channel. I’d also want the activity history to make it obvious which platforms were handled together.

Yes, it should at least respect the obvious platform limits like character counts, media size, and whether a link preview or mention format will work on that network. I’d expect Mashbot to automatically warn if a version won’t fit or may display poorly, but not to rewrite the message in a way that changes meaning without review. The team should still be able to tailor hashtags, mentions, and link placement per network before publishing.

It depends on the severity. If it’s likely to fail or get truncated in a way that would make the message unusable, Mashbot should block scheduling until it’s fixed. If it’s only a cosmetic issue or a mild formatting risk, then it can let the team proceed, but it should make the warning very clear so someone consciously accepts it.

Typically they’d create the campaign, connect the relevant social accounts, draft the content, get it reviewed by an approver if needed, and then schedule it to go out across the selected networks. After that, they’d use Mashbot to watch responses, handle any keyword alerts, and look back at the campaign history to see what happened. It feels easy when the workflow is simple and clear, the roles are obvious, and they can make network-specific tweaks without jumping around too much; it feels frustrating when approvals are confusing, updates are hard to coordinate, or they have to fix the same content repeatedly for different platforms.

It should definitely be more guided for new or occasional users, with templates and step-by-step prompts so they don’t have to know the whole process upfront. I’d also want plain-language explanations around approvals, scheduling, and network-specific warnings, because those are the areas people are most likely to stumble on. Risky actions like publishing immediately, changing connected accounts, or overriding a blackout should be harder to do by mistake, while routine drafting and scheduling should stay easy.

Mashbot should surface the main response activity on each channel, keyword hits tied to the campaign, and a clear history of what was posted, approved, changed, and when it went live. It should also highlight anything unusual, like a surge in mentions, a negative comment pattern, or a missed scheduled post, so the team can react quickly. I’d expect routine noise to be grouped or suppressed, but important alerts should be escalated to the right role, especially if they affect an active campaign or a high-priority account.

Mashbot should let them deviate, but only with clear guidance and warnings about what they’re bypassing. If an approval is missing, it should stop them from publishing until the right person reviews it, unless there’s some approved exception process already in place. For unusual network combinations or skipping ahead, it should keep the workflow flexible, but make it obvious that they’re leaving the standard path so they don’t accidentally create a bad setup.

It should check whether the user has the right role to make that change, whether the campaign is already past a point where the change would affect published content, and whether any required approvals are missing. If the deviation could break a platform rule, cause a post to fail, or bypass a required review, it should block or at least require a very explicit confirmation. If it’s just a workflow shortcut that doesn’t affect compliance or publishing safety, then a warning is enough and they can continue.

It should suppress low-value noise like routine likes, standard positive replies, or repeated duplicates that don’t need action. It should escalate things like a spike in negative sentiment, a public complaint, a keyword tied to a sensitive issue, a failed scheduled post, or anything that looks like a platform or account access problem. For a high-priority account, the escalation should go to the approver or publisher on duty, and probably also whoever owns that account internally so it can be handled quickly.

If it’s a normal operational issue, like a failed post or a customer reply that just needs action, I’d notify the on-duty approver or publisher first and keep it tight. If the issue is customer-facing, reputational, or could affect the whole account, then the internal account owner should also be alerted because they usually need visibility and decision-making power. Backup contacts should only come in when the primary people don’t respond within a set window, or if the issue is severe enough that waiting would be risky.

It should widen the alert if the issue is public-facing, could damage the brand, involves a sensitive keyword, or looks like an access or security problem. If it’s just a routine workflow failure, I’d keep it with the on-duty person unless they don’t respond quickly. The order should be primary on-duty approver or publisher first, then the account owner if it needs judgment or escalation, and then backup contacts only after a short timeout or if the issue is serious enough that we can’t wait.

Mashbot should respect the account’s region settings and any policy tags on the message or campaign, so content only appears to people who are allowed to see it. If a message is tied to a consent restriction, legal hold, or regional limitation, it should be masked or hidden from unauthorized users and still logged for audit purposes. For keyword monitoring, it should only surface the alert details to the roles and regions that are permitted to handle that type of content, rather than showing it broadly to everyone.

Mashbot should keep normal drafting and scheduled posting as simple as possible, but add friction when the action can affect a live audience or a restricted account. If someone wants to publish immediately, switch the connected account, or override a blackout window, it should check their role, whether the content is already approved, and whether the destination network has any timing or policy restrictions; if any of those are risky, it should ask for a clear confirmation or block the action. For routine scheduled posts that are already approved and within policy, it shouldn’t slow people down with extra steps.

It should look at three things mainly: whether the person has permission for that action, whether the content is already approved and safe to publish, and whether the target account or time window has any active restriction. If all three are clean, it can allow it; if the action is unusual but still acceptable, it should require an extra confirmation; if it would bypass policy, go out on the wrong account, or violate a blackout or legal restriction, it should block it entirely.
